medical.title: Congenital syphilis rates soared in US newborns from 2012 to 2022
medical.summary: Congenital syphilis rates among U.S. newborns increased nearly sixfold from 2012 to 2022, according to a new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. The data show rising rates across all demographics and income levels, with the sharpest increases among Native Americans.

medical.title: Precision RNA therapy offers hope for brain receptor disorders
medical.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Academia Sinica in Taiwan have developed an experimental RNA-based treatment that prevents brain damage and improves learning, memory and social behavior in mice carrying a rare genetic mutation associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability.

medical.title: Study measures impact of pandemic stress on gun violence spike
medical.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic coincided with one of the most dramatic swings in homicide in modern American history.

medical.title: Survey on COVID-19 smell loss reveals over 50% of respondents still have symptoms after 5 years
medical.summary: Since the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at Virginia Commonwealth University's School of Medicine have maintained a national database of patients affected by COVID-19-related smell loss. Their latest survey shows that more than half of respondents are still impacted by smell dysfunction five years after initial infection.

medical.title: Engineered hydrogel could make testicular reconstruction feel more natural
medical.summary: Researchers at UBC's Okanagan and Vancouver campuses are developing a softer testicular implant that could offer patients a more natural feel following surgical reconstruction.

medical.title: Intensified liver-directed radionuclide therapy shows promise for patients with metastatic neuroendocrine tumors
medical.summary: Combining intraarterial and intravenous administration of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) can selectively intensify treatment for liver-dominant metastatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) while still effectively delivering treatment throughout the whole body. This hybrid approach safely delivered over three times more radiation directly to liver metastases, resulting in encouraging tumor responses among patients. This research was published online in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine.

medical.title: Where will Ebola spread next? Travel patterns offer clues
medical.summary: How many trips have you squeezed into the past 10 days? Whether you're in Boston or across the globe, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, your daily routine keeps you on the move. Between seven work commutes, a couple of grocery runs, a pharmacy stop and weekend dinner with friends, you can cover a lot of ground.

medical.title: Scientists breed a 'pan-African' malaria parasite to build a better whole-parasite malaria vaccine
medical.summary: Researchers have created a hybrid malaria parasite that combines the manufacturing advantages of the strain used in every current whole-parasite malaria vaccine with the much higher liver infectivity of a parasite collected recently in East Africa. The work is published in JCI Insight.

medical.title: Q&A: Rethinking immunity beyond 'strong' and 'weak'
medical.summary: Melinda Fagan, professor in the Department of Philosophy at the University of Utah, where she holds the Sterling M. McMurrin Chair, proposed in a recent paper a new approach to understanding immunity for both experts and nonexperts, which could help address vaccine hesitancy in a science-leery public.

medical.title: Waves that clear waste from the brain during sleep are impaired in older adults
medical.summary: As people age, they may sleep for shorter periods and wake up more frequently during the night. In addition to those disruptions, MIT researchers have now discovered that a process responsible for flushing waste from the brain during sleep is commonly impaired in older people.

medical.title: Hamster hibernation study offers clues to Alzheimer's disease
medical.summary: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have discovered that hibernation triggers changes in brain cells that partially resemble those in Alzheimer's disease. Studying golden hamsters, the team identified changes in gene expression across the hibernation cycle, which resemble those associated with the accumulation of amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's.

medical.title: Vitamin D may help control lung inflammation during flu infection, study in mice suggests
medical.summary: Vitamin D may help the body fight influenza by controlling inflammation and the amount of virus in the lungs, according to a study in mice led by researchers at Penn State.

medical.title: Most new parents have intrusive thoughts about their baby being harmed: It's OK to talk about it
medical.summary: Telling your friends and family you're pregnant will earn you an avalanche of advice. Yet few parents will ever be told about a common experience that can impact the parents' long-term mental health: perinatal intrusive thoughts.

medical.title: Why exercise has become a key part of cancer treatment
medical.summary: Scientists have long known that regular exercise decreases the risk of developing many types of cancer. But last year, results from a large, randomized clinical trial of patients with colon cancer definitively showed what many observational studies and animal research had been hinting at for decades: People who exercise following cancer treatment have a better chance of surviving the disease and a lower likelihood of recurrence.

medical.title: GPs are now 'prescribing' time in nature. Is it likely to improve your health?
medical.summary: Imagine visiting your primary care doctor for your physical or mental health and leaving with a prescription to spend more time outdoors.

medical.title: Label-free imaging tracks lipid storage in living liver organoids
medical.summary: Fat accumulation in liver cells is central to several metabolic disorders, but observing the process in living tissue models remains difficult. Fluorescent labels and stains can provide detailed images, but they may disrupt cells or capture only selected time points. A label-free approach for tracking changes in lipid storage over time in three-dimensional mouse liver organoids is reported in Biophotonics Discovery.

medical.title: Sustained clinical responses seen with neuroimmune modulation for rheumatoid arthritis
medical.summary: Twenty-four-month data show sustained clinical responses for patients receiving neuroimmune modulation therapy for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology, held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

medical.title: Stomach cancer is changing: An expert explains surgical approaches
medical.summary: Sometimes innovation in cancer care means developing something entirely new. Other times, it means returning to an old idea with the knowledge and tools to make it work better. Both are happening in stomach cancer surgery, says Travis Grotz, M.D., a Mayo Clinic surgical oncologist who specializes in treating stomach cancer.

medical.title: How the brain rapidly learns to interpret ambiguous images
medical.summary: Both humans and image recognition algorithms can take time to identify the objects and scenes depicted in some images. Emblematic examples of this phenomenon are Mooney images, pictures that are intentionally reduced to patches of black and white, with no shades of gray.

medical.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
medical.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.

medical.title: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy
medical.summary: A study of more than 750,000 pregnancies found that early exposure to Ozempic, Wegovy, and similar drugs was not linked to increased pregnancy complications when used for weight loss, but was associated with a higher risk of premature birth when prescribed for diabetes. The surprising difference suggests that diabetes itself may be driving the risk, although researchers caution that the drugs' safety during pregnancy remains uncertain.

medical.title: Mobile app and telemonitoring improve quality of life and symptoms in patients with heart failure
medical.summary: A telemedicine-based management program was well accepted among patients with heart failure and improved their quality of life and self-care, according to results presented today at ESC Digital & AI Summit 2026.

medical.title: Taking a closer look at stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation
medical.summary: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), one of the most common heart rhythm disorders, are at increased risk of ischemic stroke, a stroke caused by a blood clot blocking blood flow to the brain, as well as blood clots that can travel to other parts of the body.

medical.title: A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that fasting for just 24 hours increases a beneficial gut bacterium that helps the intestines regenerate after radiation damage. The preclinical findings could pave the way for new treatments that protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without requiring patients to fast.

medical.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

science.title: Climate could force more than 200 billion from homes: U.N. migration chief
science.summary: Climate change could force more than 200 billion people from their homes even as countries spend billions on securing their borders, the head of the U.N.'s migration body said Friday.

science.title: Who lives in a sponge under the sea? Tiny Caribbean fish and their microscopic neighbors
science.summary: Two new studies involving Newcastle University marine scientist Dr. Theresa Rueger have highlighted how the tusked goby's relationship with its host sponge shapes almost every aspect of its life. Rueger, a senior lecturer in tropical marine sciences at Newcastle University's School of Natural and Environmental Sciences, is senior author of one study and co-author of the other, which together uncover the influence of sponges on the tiny Caribbean reef fish's social behavior, growth, reproduction and microbiome.

science.title: From stimulation to suppression: How nitrogen addition changes soil respiration over time
science.summary: Soil respiration (Rs), the efflux of CO₂ from soils to the atmosphere driven by root and microbial activity, is one of the largest terrestrial carbon fluxes and a primary determinant of net carbon sequestration. The important role of nitrogen in driving terrestrial carbon sequestration has long been recognized. However, the role of nitrogen in the temporal dynamics of Rs has not been well understood.

science.title: How Chinese brewers refined their booze 5,000 years ago
science.summary: More than 5,000 years ago, brewers in eastern China appear to have used red mold to make rice alcohol, then strained the drink through cloth. Microscopic residues on ancient pottery show evidence of both the fermentation method and the filtering process to separate the liquid from leftover grain.

science.title: Kindergarten teachers offer cognitive help during outdoor play but fall short on emotional and social support
science.summary: A study in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development of teachers' behavior during outdoor play at kindergarten has identified a gap between the support children need and the help educators provide, particularly in emotional and social development.

science.title: Self-learning AI separates particle jets from background noise in simulated heavy-ion collisions
science.summary: A team of physicists and computer scientists led by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Brookhaven National Laboratory developed a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach that learns on its own to separate important high-energy particle jet signals from the enormous background of particles recorded in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, where two beams of heavy ions collide at near the speed of light.

science.title: Colorful fish reveal how species stay distinct despite interbreeding
science.summary: Vividly colored fish dwelling at the bottom of shallow Midwestern streams may help biologists understand the evolutionary mechanisms by which species remain distinct despite their similarities and overlapping ranges. Orangethroat and rainbow darters regularly interbreed where their ranges overlap, yet—millions of years after they first diverged—they remain separate species.

science.title: Rh₃ clusters balance activity and butene selectivity in butane dehydrogenation
science.summary: Scientists from the Institute of Metal Research (IMR) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with researchers from Peking University and Chongqing University, have demonstrated how the geometry and electronic properties of subnanometer rhodium (Rh) active sites shape C–H activation, product desorption and C–C bond cleavage during butane dehydrogenation.

science.title: Heat drives electron orbital currents, revealing first experimental evidence of orbital Nernst effect
science.summary: Researchers at National Taiwan University (NTU) have reported the first experimental evidence of heat-current-driven transverse accumulation of electrons' orbital angular momentum, a phenomenon known as the orbital Nernst effect. The study was recently published in Nature Communications.

science.title: Scientists successfully swap all fish products in aquafeed to boost sustainable fish farming
science.summary: Global fish production and consumption have hit new heights, according to the United Nations. People worldwide are consuming much more fish per capita, and more than 23 million people now work in the aquaculture industry. That booming business is putting pressure on the world's oceans.

science.title: Outbursts from a Massive Star
science.summary: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star located in the galaxy shown in this image released on Nov. 9, 2026. The volatile star, known as AT 2016blu, is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, located about 30 million light-years from Earth. Astronomers estimate the […]

science.title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
science.summary: Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII, the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of […]

science.title: Direct observation of a submarine landslide reveals seafloor processes
science.summary: Submarine landslides have significant implications for marine ecology and infrastructure, yet these unpredictable events have remained challenging to study. New research co-led by Newcastle University's Dr. Sanem Acikalin and involving an international team of collaborators from 10 institutions has provided the first direct observations of these elusive events.

science.title: Study reveals mechanisms to sustain stable crop yields under long-term drip irrigation in arid regions
science.summary: Combining drip irrigation during the growing season with autumn or winter irrigation can help control soil salinity and sustain high, stable crop yields in the arid regions of northwestern China, according to a new study.

science.title: WheatAI could speed wheat breeding and help farmers assess crops
science.summary: Wheat researchers at South Dakota State University are perfecting an AI-powered web application designed to speed the work of wheat breeders and equip farmers with a more accurate tool for making decisions.

science.title: Fish prove every pregnancy is a battle: Unexpected evidence for the food fight between mothers and babies
science.summary: Left to their own devices, babies in the womb would suck their mothers dry. A developing baby benefits from taking as many essential nutrients as possible, but evolutionary theory predicts that to survive pregnancy, mothers need to keep some of these nutrients for themselves.

science.title: Oregon logs its first H5N1 case in cows; farmers' union says human avian flu cases underreported in Washington
science.summary: Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (USDA's APHIS) announced the first detection of H5N1 avian flu in a dairy herd in Oregon.

science.title: Young green turtles find refuge in man-made lagoon in protected UAE wetland
science.summary: A protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has become an oasis for young sea turtles, new research shows. The study tracked nine juvenile green turtles (shell length less than 60 cm (24 inches)) and found they were "highly resident" in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area—spending over 80% of their time there.

science.title: Optical system maps multiple infrared fields onto one small detector
science.summary: Researchers from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed an optical system that focuses light from several subfields onto a single small-format detector. By analyzing field-dependent spot shapes, the system identifies which subfield an isolated infrared target comes from. In sequence-level tests, it identified the correct field in about 89% of cases. The study is published in Optics and Laser Technology.

science.title: Baby corals go house-hunting, gaining swimming skills as they grow
science.summary: Coral reefs are beautiful and important, both for humans and for marine biodiversity. Corals are living creatures, although they appear to remain fixed in one place, catching small crustaceans and other tasty morsels that drift past.

science.title: Why climate anxiety makes some youth take action, while others freeze
science.summary: While young people are constantly exposed to news about climate change, their resulting anxiety does not always translate into environmental action. A new study published in Climate reveals that the relationship between climate distress and climate action is highly complex. While worry pushes some youth to seek solutions, it causes others to freeze up.

science.title: Double axes and coarse pottery reveal connections across the Rhine 5,000 years ago
science.summary: The Rhine, as the boundary between Western and Central Europe, appears to be a constant feature of European history. As early as the late fourth and early third millennia B.C., the traces of human activity east and west of the river differed. Archaeologists have long concluded that the river was a kind of barrier at that time, just as it has been in more recent centuries.

science.title: Microscopic solar panels could help shape 3D-printed biological tissue
science.summary: Bioprinting uses living cells and molecular signals to produce biological tissues and even whole organs, building them layer by layer in the lab. To keep the bioink, or blend of cells and materials that power this printing, correctly aligned to grow a target tissue, researchers use electricity. However, this typically requires bulky electronic interfaces and invasive wiring.

science.title: New research reveals when humor helps—and hurts—recruitment success
science.summary: Humor is becoming an increasingly popular feature of job advertisements, with employers using it to stand out, capture attention and attract potential candidates.

science.title: Oʻahu infrastructure threatened by tipping point in sea-level rise impacts
science.summary: A new comprehensive study by researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi (UH) at Mānoa Climate Resilience Collaborative reveals that traditional sea-level rise models, which account only for rising ocean waters, drastically underestimate the true threat to coastal infrastructure on Oʻahu, Hawai'i.

environment.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
environment.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

environment.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos
environment.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman took a moment longer than usual to look closely at a bean that was sprouting in his studio. “There was this one bean that sort of had this incredibly elegant curve, and I thought, ‘God, that’s exactly like the flamingo from like 15 years ago,’” Zuckerman tells Mongabay in a video call. […]

environment.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
environment.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

environment.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
environment.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.summary: Climate change could force more than 200 billion people from their homes even as countries spend billions on securing their borders, the head of the U.N.'s migration body said Friday.

mix_items.title: Congenital syphilis rates soared in US newborns from 2012 to 2022
mix_items.summary: Congenital syphilis rates among U.S. newborns increased nearly sixfold from 2012 to 2022, according to a new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. The data show rising rates across all demographics and income levels, with the sharpest increases among Native Americans.

mix_items.title: Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco
mix_items.summary: Peste 500 de copii au participat la activități de educație nonformală și wellbeing derulate de Fundația Inocenți cu sprijinul Pepco România. The post Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Who lives in a sponge under the sea? Tiny Caribbean fish and their microscopic neighbors
mix_items.summary: Two new studies involving Newcastle University marine scientist Dr. Theresa Rueger have highlighted how the tusked goby's relationship with its host sponge shapes almost every aspect of its life. Rueger, a senior lecturer in tropical marine sciences at Newcastle University's School of Natural and Environmental Sciences, is senior author of one study and co-author of the other, which together uncover the influence of sponges on the tiny Caribbean reef fish's social behavior, growth, reproduction and microbiome.

mix_items.title: From stimulation to suppression: How nitrogen addition changes soil respiration over time
mix_items.summary: Soil respiration (Rs), the efflux of CO₂ from soils to the atmosphere driven by root and microbial activity, is one of the largest terrestrial carbon fluxes and a primary determinant of net carbon sequestration. The important role of nitrogen in driving terrestrial carbon sequestration has long been recognized. However, the role of nitrogen in the temporal dynamics of Rs has not been well understood.

mix_items.title: How Chinese brewers refined their booze 5,000 years ago
mix_items.summary: More than 5,000 years ago, brewers in eastern China appear to have used red mold to make rice alcohol, then strained the drink through cloth. Microscopic residues on ancient pottery show evidence of both the fermentation method and the filtering process to separate the liquid from leftover grain.

mix_items.title: Kindergarten teachers offer cognitive help during outdoor play but fall short on emotional and social support
mix_items.summary: A study in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development of teachers' behavior during outdoor play at kindergarten has identified a gap between the support children need and the help educators provide, particularly in emotional and social development.

mix_items.title: Precision RNA therapy offers hope for brain receptor disorders
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Academia Sinica in Taiwan have developed an experimental RNA-based treatment that prevents brain damage and improves learning, memory and social behavior in mice carrying a rare genetic mutation associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability.

mix_items.title: Self-learning AI separates particle jets from background noise in simulated heavy-ion collisions
mix_items.summary: A team of physicists and computer scientists led by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Brookhaven National Laboratory developed a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach that learns on its own to separate important high-energy particle jet signals from the enormous background of particles recorded in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, where two beams of heavy ions collide at near the speed of light.

mix_items.title: Study measures impact of pandemic stress on gun violence spike
mix_items.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic coincided with one of the most dramatic swings in homicide in modern American history.

mix_items.title: Survey on COVID-19 smell loss reveals over 50% of respondents still have symptoms after 5 years
mix_items.summary: Since the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at Virginia Commonwealth University's School of Medicine have maintained a national database of patients affected by COVID-19-related smell loss. Their latest survey shows that more than half of respondents are still impacted by smell dysfunction five years after initial infection.

mix_items.title: Engineered hydrogel could make testicular reconstruction feel more natural
mix_items.summary: Researchers at UBC's Okanagan and Vancouver campuses are developing a softer testicular implant that could offer patients a more natural feel following surgical reconstruction.

mix_items.title: Colorful fish reveal how species stay distinct despite interbreeding
mix_items.summary: Vividly colored fish dwelling at the bottom of shallow Midwestern streams may help biologists understand the evolutionary mechanisms by which species remain distinct despite their similarities and overlapping ranges. Orangethroat and rainbow darters regularly interbreed where their ranges overlap, yet—millions of years after they first diverged—they remain separate species.

mix_items.title: Rh₃ clusters balance activity and butene selectivity in butane dehydrogenation
mix_items.summary: Scientists from the Institute of Metal Research (IMR) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with researchers from Peking University and Chongqing University, have demonstrated how the geometry and electronic properties of subnanometer rhodium (Rh) active sites shape C–H activation, product desorption and C–C bond cleavage during butane dehydrogenation.

mix_items.title: Heat drives electron orbital currents, revealing first experimental evidence of orbital Nernst effect
mix_items.summary: Researchers at National Taiwan University (NTU) have reported the first experimental evidence of heat-current-driven transverse accumulation of electrons' orbital angular momentum, a phenomenon known as the orbital Nernst effect. The study was recently published in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Scientists successfully swap all fish products in aquafeed to boost sustainable fish farming
mix_items.summary: Global fish production and consumption have hit new heights, according to the United Nations. People worldwide are consuming much more fish per capita, and more than 23 million people now work in the aquaculture industry. That booming business is putting pressure on the world's oceans.

mix_items.title: Intensified liver-directed radionuclide therapy shows promise for patients with metastatic neuroendocrine tumors
mix_items.summary: Combining intraarterial and intravenous administration of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) can selectively intensify treatment for liver-dominant metastatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) while still effectively delivering treatment throughout the whole body. This hybrid approach safely delivered over three times more radiation directly to liver metastases, resulting in encouraging tumor responses among patients. This research was published online in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine.

mix_items.title: Outbursts from a Massive Star
mix_items.summary: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star located in the galaxy shown in this image released on Nov. 9, 2026. The volatile star, known as AT 2016blu, is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, located about 30 million light-years from Earth. Astronomers estimate the […]

mix_items.title: Where will Ebola spread next? Travel patterns offer clues
mix_items.summary: How many trips have you squeezed into the past 10 days? Whether you're in Boston or across the globe, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, your daily routine keeps you on the move. Between seven work commutes, a couple of grocery runs, a pharmacy stop and weekend dinner with friends, you can cover a lot of ground.

mix_items.title: Scientists breed a 'pan-African' malaria parasite to build a better whole-parasite malaria vaccine
mix_items.summary: Researchers have created a hybrid malaria parasite that combines the manufacturing advantages of the strain used in every current whole-parasite malaria vaccine with the much higher liver infectivity of a parasite collected recently in East Africa. The work is published in JCI Insight.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Rethinking immunity beyond 'strong' and 'weak'
mix_items.summary: Melinda Fagan, professor in the Department of Philosophy at the University of Utah, where she holds the Sterling M. McMurrin Chair, proposed in a recent paper a new approach to understanding immunity for both experts and nonexperts, which could help address vaccine hesitancy in a science-leery public.

mix_items.title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
mix_items.summary: Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII, the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of […]

mix_items.title: Direct observation of a submarine landslide reveals seafloor processes
mix_items.summary: Submarine landslides have significant implications for marine ecology and infrastructure, yet these unpredictable events have remained challenging to study. New research co-led by Newcastle University's Dr. Sanem Acikalin and involving an international team of collaborators from 10 institutions has provided the first direct observations of these elusive events.

mix_items.title: Waves that clear waste from the brain during sleep are impaired in older adults
mix_items.summary: As people age, they may sleep for shorter periods and wake up more frequently during the night. In addition to those disruptions, MIT researchers have now discovered that a process responsible for flushing waste from the brain during sleep is commonly impaired in older people.

mix_items.title: Study reveals mechanisms to sustain stable crop yields under long-term drip irrigation in arid regions
mix_items.summary: Combining drip irrigation during the growing season with autumn or winter irrigation can help control soil salinity and sustain high, stable crop yields in the arid regions of northwestern China, according to a new study.

mix_items.title: WheatAI could speed wheat breeding and help farmers assess crops
mix_items.summary: Wheat researchers at South Dakota State University are perfecting an AI-powered web application designed to speed the work of wheat breeders and equip farmers with a more accurate tool for making decisions.

mix_items.title: Hamster hibernation study offers clues to Alzheimer's disease
mix_items.summary: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have discovered that hibernation triggers changes in brain cells that partially resemble those in Alzheimer's disease. Studying golden hamsters, the team identified changes in gene expression across the hibernation cycle, which resemble those associated with the accumulation of amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's.

mix_items.title: Fish prove every pregnancy is a battle: Unexpected evidence for the food fight between mothers and babies
mix_items.summary: Left to their own devices, babies in the womb would suck their mothers dry. A developing baby benefits from taking as many essential nutrients as possible, but evolutionary theory predicts that to survive pregnancy, mothers need to keep some of these nutrients for themselves.

mix_items.title: Vitamin D may help control lung inflammation during flu infection, study in mice suggests
mix_items.summary: Vitamin D may help the body fight influenza by controlling inflammation and the amount of virus in the lungs, according to a study in mice led by researchers at Penn State.

mix_items.title: Oregon logs its first H5N1 case in cows; farmers' union says human avian flu cases underreported in Washington
mix_items.summary: Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (USDA's APHIS) announced the first detection of H5N1 avian flu in a dairy herd in Oregon.

mix_items.title: Young green turtles find refuge in man-made lagoon in protected UAE wetland
mix_items.summary: A protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has become an oasis for young sea turtles, new research shows. The study tracked nine juvenile green turtles (shell length less than 60 cm (24 inches)) and found they were "highly resident" in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area—spending over 80% of their time there.

mix_items.title: Optical system maps multiple infrared fields onto one small detector
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed an optical system that focuses light from several subfields onto a single small-format detector. By analyzing field-dependent spot shapes, the system identifies which subfield an isolated infrared target comes from. In sequence-level tests, it identified the correct field in about 89% of cases. The study is published in Optics and Laser Technology.

mix_items.title: Baby corals go house-hunting, gaining swimming skills as they grow
mix_items.summary: Coral reefs are beautiful and important, both for humans and for marine biodiversity. Corals are living creatures, although they appear to remain fixed in one place, catching small crustaceans and other tasty morsels that drift past.

mix_items.title: Most new parents have intrusive thoughts about their baby being harmed: It's OK to talk about it
mix_items.summary: Telling your friends and family you're pregnant will earn you an avalanche of advice. Yet few parents will ever be told about a common experience that can impact the parents' long-term mental health: perinatal intrusive thoughts.

mix_items.title: Why climate anxiety makes some youth take action, while others freeze
mix_items.summary: While young people are constantly exposed to news about climate change, their resulting anxiety does not always translate into environmental action. A new study published in Climate reveals that the relationship between climate distress and climate action is highly complex. While worry pushes some youth to seek solutions, it causes others to freeze up.

mix_items.title: Double axes and coarse pottery reveal connections across the Rhine 5,000 years ago
mix_items.summary: The Rhine, as the boundary between Western and Central Europe, appears to be a constant feature of European history. As early as the late fourth and early third millennia B.C., the traces of human activity east and west of the river differed. Archaeologists have long concluded that the river was a kind of barrier at that time, just as it has been in more recent centuries.

mix_items.title: Why exercise has become a key part of cancer treatment
mix_items.summary: Scientists have long known that regular exercise decreases the risk of developing many types of cancer. But last year, results from a large, randomized clinical trial of patients with colon cancer definitively showed what many observational studies and animal research had been hinting at for decades: People who exercise following cancer treatment have a better chance of surviving the disease and a lower likelihood of recurrence.

mix_items.title: Microscopic solar panels could help shape 3D-printed biological tissue
mix_items.summary: Bioprinting uses living cells and molecular signals to produce biological tissues and even whole organs, building them layer by layer in the lab. To keep the bioink, or blend of cells and materials that power this printing, correctly aligned to grow a target tissue, researchers use electricity. However, this typically requires bulky electronic interfaces and invasive wiring.

mix_items.title: New research reveals when humor helps—and hurts—recruitment success
mix_items.summary: Humor is becoming an increasingly popular feature of job advertisements, with employers using it to stand out, capture attention and attract potential candidates.

mix_items.title: Oʻahu infrastructure threatened by tipping point in sea-level rise impacts
mix_items.summary: A new comprehensive study by researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi (UH) at Mānoa Climate Resilience Collaborative reveals that traditional sea-level rise models, which account only for rising ocean waters, drastically underestimate the true threat to coastal infrastructure on Oʻahu, Hawai'i.

mix_items.title: GPs are now 'prescribing' time in nature. Is it likely to improve your health?
mix_items.summary: Imagine visiting your primary care doctor for your physical or mental health and leaving with a prescription to spend more time outdoors.

mix_items.title: Label-free imaging tracks lipid storage in living liver organoids
mix_items.summary: Fat accumulation in liver cells is central to several metabolic disorders, but observing the process in living tissue models remains difficult. Fluorescent labels and stains can provide detailed images, but they may disrupt cells or capture only selected time points. A label-free approach for tracking changes in lipid storage over time in three-dimensional mouse liver organoids is reported in Biophotonics Discovery.

mix_items.title: Sustained clinical responses seen with neuroimmune modulation for rheumatoid arthritis
mix_items.summary: Twenty-four-month data show sustained clinical responses for patients receiving neuroimmune modulation therapy for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology, held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

mix_items.title: Stomach cancer is changing: An expert explains surgical approaches
mix_items.summary: Sometimes innovation in cancer care means developing something entirely new. Other times, it means returning to an old idea with the knowledge and tools to make it work better. Both are happening in stomach cancer surgery, says Travis Grotz, M.D., a Mayo Clinic surgical oncologist who specializes in treating stomach cancer.

mix_items.title: How the brain rapidly learns to interpret ambiguous images
mix_items.summary: Both humans and image recognition algorithms can take time to identify the objects and scenes depicted in some images. Emblematic examples of this phenomenon are Mooney images, pictures that are intentionally reduced to patches of black and white, with no shades of gray.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
mix_items.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.

mix_items.title: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy
mix_items.summary: A study of more than 750,000 pregnancies found that early exposure to Ozempic, Wegovy, and similar drugs was not linked to increased pregnancy complications when used for weight loss, but was associated with a higher risk of premature birth when prescribed for diabetes. The surprising difference suggests that diabetes itself may be driving the risk, although researchers caution that the drugs' safety during pregnancy remains uncertain.

mix_items.title: Mobile app and telemonitoring improve quality of life and symptoms in patients with heart failure
mix_items.summary: A telemedicine-based management program was well accepted among patients with heart failure and improved their quality of life and self-care, according to results presented today at ESC Digital & AI Summit 2026.

mix_items.title: Taking a closer look at stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation
mix_items.summary: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), one of the most common heart rhythm disorders, are at increased risk of ischemic stroke, a stroke caused by a blood clot blocking blood flow to the brain, as well as blood clots that can travel to other parts of the body.

mix_items.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
mix_items.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

mix_items.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos
mix_items.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman took a moment longer than usual to look closely at a bean that was sprouting in his studio. “There was this one bean that sort of had this incredibly elegant curve, and I thought, ‘God, that’s exactly like the flamingo from like 15 years ago,’” Zuckerman tells Mongabay in a video call. […]

mix_items.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
mix_items.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

mix_items.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
mix_items.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. It also says it has hired an outside firm to investigate after an Indonesian migrant fishers’ union demanded a binding labor agreement with the company. In a statement sent to Mongabay on Nov. […]

mix_items.title: Weird and wonderful wildlife revealed in underexplored mountains
mix_items.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

mix_items.title: Investigation continues in Indonesia after first conviction in 3-ton pangolin trafficking case
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesian investigators say they expect further developments in a major wildlife trafficking case after an intermediary was sentenced to nine years in prison over the discovery of 3.05 metric tons of pangolin scales at the country’s largest port in February this year. “We’re continuing to expand the investigation to dismantle this illegal […]

mix_items.title: A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that fasting for just 24 hours increases a beneficial gut bacterium that helps the intestines regenerate after radiation damage. The preclinical findings could pave the way for new treatments that protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without requiring patients to fast.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
